claims: {{canonicalName}} begins in an elevated bilateral floor bridge and alternates one controlled foot lift and replacement while the pelvis stays elevated, then ends with a controlled bilateral return.
This excludes a bilateral rise-and-return bridge, hip thrust, walkout, single-leg repetitions, static hold, testing, and forced range.
Alternating foot lift changes the support count and ordered action while the bridge remains elevated.
Support, alternating sequence, range, pause, cadence, external load, and total side count must be declared rather than inferred.
Record hip extension, hip flexion, foot support, pelvis, trunk, hip, knee, and spine roles as task mechanics, not isolated-muscle or clinical claims.
No universal activation ranking, foot position, pelvis height, or therapeutic outcome is established.
A valid candidate cycle retains an elevated bridge while one foot lifts and returns under control before the other side.
Lumbar extension, pelvis drop, or rotation does not create extra valid range.
Difficulty scores describe exercise complexity and physical demand only, never participant skill, proficiency, age, or classification.
The elevated alternating-support task has more coordination and pelvic-control demand than the bilateral rise-return baseline; independent calibration remains required.
Repeated reduced-support bridge work can change posterior-chain exposure; dose and surrounding work determine fatigue and recovery.
Track left/right lifts, bridge range, tempo, compensation, cramp, symptoms, and same-session hip-extension work.
Use a clear stable floor or mat, space to lie and exit, optional padding, and a clear stop signal.
Readiness and session fit are workout inputs, not participant labels on this exercise card.
Bridge task interpretation depends on explicit setup and dose; this candidate has no universal volume, range, or recovery claim.
Stop before pain, persistent cramp, pelvis/trunk compensation, breath-holding, or loss of controlled foot replacement.
Instructions must name the floor base, bilateral bridge, small alternating foot lift, quiet pelvis/trunk, controlled replacement, and bilateral exit.
Reduce lift height, bridge range, cycle count, or select another reviewed task before forcing control.
Instruction, stable surface, communication, and progressive exposure are safeguards.
Stop for pain, new symptoms, dizziness, persistent cramp, unsafe surface, or uncorrectable pelvic/trunk loss.
Use {{canonicalName}} only when the exact alternating elevated-support task fits the session and fatigue budget; it guarantees no transfer or outcome.
Any change to support, foot lift sequence, load, range, pause, cadence, dose, or substitution reruns selection, logistics, duration, fatigue, and validation.
Athlete support should show the base, quiet pelvis, small lift, controlled replacement, bilateral return, self-check, and stop prompt.
Captions, transcript, stills, audio description, exact media match, and demonstration quality remain human-review requirements.
Observe exact base, side sequence, foot pressure, pelvis/trunk organisation, range, cadence, cramp, and first quality loss.
Do not diagnose inhibition or make a different bridge task an automatic substitute.
Candidate supports include padding, reduced range, lower lift, fewer cycles, longer rest, still cues, and another reviewed task when supine work is inaccessible.
Supports do not establish individual readiness or media accessibility.
Alternating march, walkout, single-leg repetition, static hold, hip thrust, and test endpoints change ordered action, support, contraction, or geometry and require separate assessment.
Foot placement, lift height, cadence, short pause, cycle count, and rest are declared delivery modifiers only under the same alternating elevated-bridge contract.
Three inherited direct YouTube URLs are retained only as unverified candidates; no playback, exact-match, accessibility, quality, reviewer, or approval claim is made.
Privacy-enhanced URLs are review artifacts only and remain non-embeddable until human verification.

assessmentSummary.identity: Glute Bridge March is an elevated bilateral floor bridge with an ordered alternating foot-lift-and-replacement sequence while the pelvis remains elevated, followed by a controlled bilateral return.
currentCardFindings: Source 65 has useful coaching notes but lacks an exact canonical cycle, fatigue contract, controlled alternates, calibration, and candidate review gates.
Alternating elevated support is distinct from the bilateral bridge, hip thrust, walkout, single-leg dynamic bridge, and static bridge hold.
